summary: Young children (ages 4-6) learn to compare how long events take (duration: quicker/slower) and when they happen (position in time: earlier/later). The core hurdle is separating DURATION from distance, speed, which event stopped last, or how much happened during an event — the classic time-speed-distance confusion, where a faster, further-travelling, or busier event is wrongly judged to take longer. Teaching uses real timed events compared side by side, with explicit talk separating 'finished later' from 'took longer'.
misconceptions: Judges duration by distance or speed — the faster/further one 'took longer' (or slower means less time)
Equates 'finished later / stopped last' with 'took more time', ignoring the start
Ties 'a long time' to how much happened rather than elapsed time

activities.title: Watch duration grow from a shared start
steps: Start two events at the same moment and watch a visible timer or growing duration-bar under each until it stops
Name which event was quicker — the one with the shorter bar/time — and say how you know
Use a slower-speed toggle to make a walker go along the SAME path at a slower walking speed, while the timer runs in real time, and watch its duration-bar grow longer than before
Say out loud: 'slower over the same way means MORE time'
Switch to a mode where the two events start at DIFFERENT times, and decide whether 'finished last' really means 'took longest'
activities.insight: Duration can be seen directly — how long something takes on the clock — separately from how fast it goes, how far it travels, or how much happens during it. Going slower over the same route takes MORE time, not less. Finishing last is not the same as taking longest when starts differ.

activities.title: Race and time real events with a common start
steps: Compare two real timed events side by side — a race, two sand-timers (e.g. 30 seconds and 1 minute), or two classroom colouring tasks
Begin both from a common start so 'who finished first' is a fair judge of who was quicker
Name which event was quicker and which was slower, and explain how you know
Set up a case where the two events start at different times and discuss why 'finished first' no longer settles who was quicker
activities.insight: When two events share a start, finishing first means quicker. When starts differ, you must consider when each began — finishing order alone does not tell you who took longer.

activities.title: Talk through events using quicker/slower/earlier/later
steps: Give live commentary on a race or on the day's events, saying who or what was quicker/slower and what happened earlier/later
Answer a questioner who asks 'Who was quicker? How do you know?' and respond to the challenge 'but he ran further — does further mean longer?'

Reason about a case like two cars where the red car goes further but the green car was still moving after the red one stopped. If both started at the same moment, the green car took more time even though it went less far. If you don't know when each started, decide what else you need to know.
Explain the difference between finishing EARLIER (where on the day) and being QUICKER (how long it took)
Place daily events (breakfast, lunch, home-time) on a timeline to anchor earlier/later
activities.insight: Quicker/slower describe how long something took (duration on a timer); earlier/later describe where an event sits on the day's timeline (position). These are different ideas and should be used in their own contexts. Going further is not the same as having taken more time. Still moving after another stopped means more time only if both started together.

activities.title: Decide quicker/slower and order by duration
steps: Given two timer pictures, choose which event was quicker
Put several events in order by how long they took
Match daily events onto a timeline using earlier/later
Answer a 'walk more slowly over the same route — more or less time?' question and explain your reasoning
activities.insight: You can judge and compare durations from timer readings, and the slower trip over the same route takes MORE time — a check on the speed-equals-less-time intuition.

checkQuestion: Set up real comparisons and listen for correct USE: (1) Two sand-timers (30 seconds and 1 minute) started together: 'Which one is quicker? How do you know?' (2) 'On Monday my walk to school takes 10 minutes. On Tuesday I walk more slowly — does Tuesday's walk take more or less time? On Wednesday it takes 8 minutes — which day was I quickest?' (3) 'We both started colouring at the same time and I finished first — who was quicker?'
checkAnswer: Identifies the shorter timer as quicker; reasons that walking more slowly over the same route takes MORE time, and that 8 minutes < 10 minutes so Wednesday was quickest; says the child who finished first (same start) was quicker. Uses quicker/slower for duration and earlier/later for position, correctly.
